✔ Your full address (including postcode)

records.transcript:
Sirs/ Ma'am,

I am writing to make a request under the Freedom of Information Act 2000.

At your earliest convenience please would you provide me copies of all
information held by Cadw relating to Great House Farm, formerly occupied by
my Buckler / Williams family, which was subject to a refusal to list and
subsequent demolition in or around the late 1980s.

Specifically, I request disclosure of the following:

1. All records, assessments, reports, site visit notes, photographs,
desk-based evaluations, or recommendations produced by or for Cadw in
relation to Great House Farm, including any material connected to decisions
not to list the building.

2. All internal correspondence (including letters, memoranda, emails, and
briefing notes) held by Cadw that relate to:
The heritage significance of Great House Farm

3. The decision not to list the building
Any consideration of archaeological, historical, or associative significance
Any communications between Cadw and third parties (including local
authorities, developers, landowners, or commercial entities) concerning
Great House Farm prior to demolition

4. Records of any archaeological notifications, alerts, or discoveries
associated with Great House Farm, whether before or after demolition,
including references to artefacts later recovered during excavations in the
early 1990s.

5. Any documentation referring to historical associations between Great
House Farm and early radio or wireless experimentation, including any
mention of Guglielmo Marconi or related activity in the Cardiff Bay /
Lavernock / surrounding area that may have been considered or dismissed.

6. Policy or guidance documents in force at the time (1980s) that governed
Cadw’s criteria for listing historic farmhouses or buildings with
associative historical value.

7. If any information is withheld, please specify the exemption relied upon
and provide the reasoning as required under the Act.

I would prefer to receive the information electronically, by email.

Please confirm receipt of this request too.

I understand that under the Freedom of Information Act you're required to
respond within 20 working days. It's not that urgent so please take the
time you need, within reason, and keep me updated where possible.

And if you have any questions, queries or concerns please feel free to
reach out to me too.

Regards,

Requester

records.transcript:
Dear HM Land Registry Customer Support,

I am writing to raise a formal concern that the registered title to land
formerly occupied by my family, first registered in the name of BP
Properties Ltd in or around November 1982, may not accurately reflect the
legal and factual position that existed at the time of first registration.

I respectfully request guidance on the appropriate procedure to apply for
the entry of a notice or restriction, and/or for rectification or
alteration of the register, on the basis that an occupied and disputed
interest was not recorded.

*Summary of relevant facts (supported by court records and contemporaneous
newspaper reporting):*

   1.

   *Long-term occupation and asserted ownership*
   My grandmother and family before her, occupied the farmhouse and
   surrounding land openly and continuously for centuries, but certainly
   decades prior to registration; without payment of rent and while asserting
   ownership. The property was maintained as our family home and farm.
   2.

   *No conclusive determination of title in 1974*
   Proceedings in July 1974 relating to possession and title were adjourned
   and never substantively determined. Further proceedings in October 1974
   were interrupted by correspondence from BP entities offering a purported
   licence to occupy. As a result, there was no final judicial determination
   in 1974 establishing BP’s title on the merits.
   3.

   *Express rejection of the purported licence*
   My grandmother expressly rejected the licence, stating that the land was
   hers. This rejection was acknowledged in later proceedings, but as having
   been communicated to BP Pension Trust Limited, not the claimant in BP Vs
   Buckler 1987 i.e. BP Properties Ltd.
   4.

   *Inconsistent treatment of BP corporate identity*
   Subsequently the rejection was discounted on the basis that it was
   addressed to BP Pension Trust Limited rather than BP Properties Ltd.
   However, in dismissing my father’s appeal to that case almost immidiately
   afterwards, the court and same judge, treated BP Pension Trust Limited and
   BP Properties Ltd as "effectively the same entity for substantive
   purposes". This inconsistency resulted in the rejection being acknowledged
   but disregarded when it favoured BP, while corporate equivalence was relied
   upon to defeat the appeal.
   5.

   *Forced removal and restraint (not abandonment)*
   My family did not abandon the property or leave by our own accord, nor
   did we fully understand what or why this was happening. In 1987, my father
   and all of us, his dependants, were forcibly removed. Contemporary
   newspaper reports state that he was also taken from a hospital bed,
   detained without criminal charge, and made subject to a restraining order
   preventing him from returning to the farm. He was not even permitted to
   retrieve personal belongings.
   6.

   *Demolition following enforced exclusion*
   While my father was later restrained from returning to occupy or defend
   our home, the farmhouse was demolished. This enforced exclusion and
   demolition rendered continued occupation impossible and removed the
   physical evidence of long-term residence.
   7.

   *Registration despite occupation and unresolved dispute*

   BP Properties Ltd was registered as proprietor in 1982, at a time when:


   - the land was occupied by my family,
   - ownership was actively disputed,
   - no court had conclusively determined title, and
   - cessation of occupation occurred only later through enforcement and
   restraint, not voluntary departure.

No notice, restriction, or record of the disputed and occupied interest
appears to have been entered on the register at first registration.

*Purpose of this correspondence*

I am not seeking to relitigate historic proceedings at this stage. I am
seeking to ensure that the land register accurately reflects interests and
disputes that existed at the time of first registration, and that the
absence of abandonment and the circumstances of enforced removal are
properly understood.

I respectfully request advice on:

   - the appropriate procedure to apply for a notice or restriction
   reflecting an omitted interest; and/or
   - the process for seeking rectification or alteration of the register
   under the Land Registration legislation applicable at the time.

Please advise on the relevant forms, evidential requirements, and next
steps.

Regards,


Requester

records.transcript:
Ms Smith,

Thanks for your reply and for explaining The National Archives’ position
regarding annotation and review of records.

I fully accept that archives do not resolve disputes and that records are
often incomplete or patchwork in character. My purpose in writing is not to
seek amendment, adjudication, or retrospective commentary, but to raise a
specific concern about how absence, silence, and fragmentation within the
archival record should be understood where material public consequences
clearly followed.

By way of clarification, my concern relates to the historical record
surrounding Great House Farm, Llandough, and the proceedings culminating in *BP
Properties Ltd v Buckler* [1987] EWCA Civ 2. In particular:

   - Ownership and occupation of the farmhouse and garden were actively
   contested in 1974, with a defence asserting adverse possession filed on
   behalf of Mary Williams, and the matter adjourned without a final
   determination of title.
   - Enforcement of earlier possession orders was deferred, a warrant was
   withdrawn on 31 October 1974, and the occupier remained in possession until
   her death in 1983.
   - Despite this, land registration, demolition (1988), and archaeological
   intervention proceeded without a High Court determination of ownership and
   without disclosure of earlier, locally known archaeological discoveries.
   - A Roman burial reportedly discovered beneath the farmhouse in 1888 by
   the occupying family appears not to have been reflected in later “rescue”
   excavations (1978–1980) or the major 1994 excavation, which treated Roman
   and early medieval burials as newly revealed.

Taken together, this produces an archival landscape in which:

   - court files relating to decisive events appear absent or incomplete;
   - later records imply finality where proceedings were in fact unresolved;
   - and the destruction of a long-occupied medieval structure occurred
   before the site’s known archaeological significance was formally
   acknowledged.

I note and appreciate your confirmation that the principal judicial series
(J 157, J 83, J 84) contain no relevant material. Given the scale of the
consequences flowing from the dispute—forced removal, demolition of an
occupied dwelling, and loss of heritage fabric—the absence of supporting
court or administrative files is itself significant for researchers.

Accordingly, I would be grateful for guidance on the following procedural
points:

   - how researchers are expected to interpret gaps or silence in the
   archival record where substantial actions plainly occurred;
   - whether related non-judicial records (for example, departmental,
   planning, regulatory, or corporate records connected to land registration,
   planning consent, or archaeological works) are more likely to sit outside

Councillor Carroll & co,

I write regarding potential gaps in the Council's planning and
record-keeping processes relating to Great House Farm, Llandough, which was
demolished in 1988 following the 1987 Court of Appeal decision in BP
Properties Ltd v Buckler.

Recent evidence suggests the Council may wish to examine its own position
on this matter, as it raises questions about procedural compliance and
record integrity that could expose the authority to wider scrutiny.

CORE ISSUES

**1. Identity and Procedural Integrity**

The 1987 judgment turned on a 1974 licence addressed to "Mrs Buckler". My
grandmother, Mary Williams, did not use or accept this designation.
Contemporaneous evidence (1978 newspaper article attached) records her
asserting ownership under her correct name.

If the 1987 court was not presented with this evidence, the judgment may
rest on an incomplete factual record. This raises procedural fairness
concerns relevant to any future review of the decision.

**2. Heritage Information and Statutory Compliance**

The site's archaeological significance was documented by 1978 (Roman
burials, monastic associations). Yet professional excavations in 1994
revealed 1,026 early medieval burials and monastic structures—findings that
should have prompted evaluation under the Ancient Monuments and
Archaeological Areas Act 1979.

Critical question: Did the Council conduct or require prior archaeological
assessment before granting permissions to demolish? If not, this represents
a potential gap in statutory process that may affect the validity of the
permissions granted.

**3. Land Registry Disclosure**

BP registered title in 1982 based on the disputed licence. The Council
should establish:
- Whether any dispute notice or heritage caution was lodged;
- Whether the Council disclosed relevant heritage information to the Land
Registry;
- What planning records exist from 1978–1988 regarding the site's known
archaeological potential.

**4. Corporate Identity Inconsistency**

During my father's appeal, the court treated BP Properties Ltd and BP
Pension Trust Ltd inconsistently—as separate entities when convenient, then
as one when dismissing his claim. This raises questions about how
thoroughly the litigation was scrutinised and whether the Council's records
reflect this uncertainty.

WHY THIS MATTERS TO THE COUNCIL

These issues go beyond a single historical dispute. They touch on:

- **Planning record integrity**: Whether heritage information was
adequately documented and acted upon;
- **Procedural compliance**: Whether statutory protections (Ancient
Monuments Act) were properly applied;
- **Institutional liability**: Whether decisions were made on incomplete or
misleading information;
- **Precedent risk**: Whether similar vulnerabilities may exist in other
historical planning decisions.

REQUESTS

I ask the Council to:

1. **Commission a review** of the planning permissions granted between
1978–1988 for Great House Farm, specifically examining what heritage and
archaeological information was available to decision-makers and how it was
handled.

2. **Refer this matter to the Monitoring Officer** for examination of
procedural compliance and record integrity.

3. **Establish** what correspondence, cautions, or dispute notices exist in
relation to this site's title or heritage status.

4. **Clarify the Council's current protocol** for handling historical title
disputes, previously unknown heritage information, or allegations of
material non-disclosure in past planning processes—to prevent recurrence.

I am not asking the Council to reverse the 1987 judgment or disturb current
residents. I am asking it to ensure its own records are accurate and its
own processes are defensible.

I attach the 1978 article and supporting documents, and am available to
meet or provide further information.

Yours faithfully,

Requester, Sgt (Ret'd)
Executor for the Manor of Llandough
[address redacted], [postcode redacted]

Thank you for contacting HM Land Registry. This is an automated response to confirm that we have received your correspondence. We aim to formally provide an acknowledgement within three working days. If you have any special requirements that mean you would like us to communicate with you in a specific way, please let us know and we will make adjustments if we can.


If you are contacting us in respect of any matters relating to property registration or have a general customer enquiry – Our team are unable to respond to any general registration enquiries or provide updates on any property applications. Please redirect your customer enquiry to our Customer Support colleagues, using any of the methods below:


  *   Online contact form: HM Land Registry Contact Us form<https://customerhelp.landregistry.gov.uk/guide-page-external/?stepid=2b31bc48-eb96-eb11-b1ac-002248413956>
  *   Website - www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry<http://www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry>
  *   Telephone
  *   English language [phone redacted]
  *   Welsh language [phone redacted]


Telephone lines are open between 08:00 and 17:00 Monday to Thursday. This does not include Bank Holidays.


  *   Post

HM Land Registry Citizen Centre
PO Box 74
Gloucester
[postcode redacted]

There is no direct contact e-mail address for Customer Support. Please use the online contact form and any responses will be issued via e-mail.

If you have made a request under the Freedom of Information Act or Environmental Information Regulations – the statutory timescale for response is 20 working days following receipt of your request.

If you have made a request in relation to your data rights, for example, a subject access request for personal data – the statutory timescale for response is one calendar month following receipt of your request.

Please note that where personal data is held on our register, it is exempt from the right of subject access under UK GDPR.

Where any personal data is held on record for a registered title, the exemption provided at Schedule 2, Part 1, Paragraph 5(1) of the Data Protection Act 2018 would be engaged.

This states:

“5(1) The listed GDPR provisions do not apply to personal data consisting of information that the controller is obliged by an enactment to make available to the public, to the extent that the application of those provisions would prevent the controller from complying with that obligation.”

Please see the section below titled 'Register information and your data protection rights' for further explanation.

If you have only copied your correspondence to us - we will not respond.

Yours sincerely

Information Rights Team
HM Land Registry

Accessing information held by HMLR on our register of title

To assist you in accessing information held by HMLR, please be aware most of the information held within our registers is open to public inspection and accessible via statutory routes of access. This means that we may be unable to provide access to this information via a Freedom of Information Act 2000 (FOIA) request.

Statutory Routes of Access to information held on Public Registers

The Land Registration Act 2002 is the principal legislation governing land registration in England and Wales. It sets out provisions for keeping a register of title to land and property, and in accordance with Section 66 & 67 of the Land Registration Act, it is a requirement that the Chief Land Registrar makes this information (including any documents held on the register of title) available for public inspection.

How to access information held on our Registers

The information you have requested is available to access under our statutory protocol under section 66 & 67 of the Land Registration Act 2002.

Search for Land and Property

Please visit our website for further information about our registers:

www.gov.uk/get-information-about-property-and-land<http://www.gov.uk/get-information-about-property-and-land>

Official Copies

For information about how to apply for official copies of documents held in relation to registered titles, and information about the types of documents available, please refer to practice guide 11:

www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies<http://www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies>

Index of proprietors’ names

Under rule 11 of the Land Registration Rules 2003 the registrar is required to keep an index of proprietors’ names which shows for each individual register the proprietor of the registered estate and the proprietor of any registered charge together with the title number. When you search the index of proprietors’ names, you will receive a list of titles that are owned by, or mortgaged to, the name that you have searched against.

For further information about this please refer to practice guide 74:

www.gov.uk/government/publications/searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names/practice-guide-74-searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names<http://www.gov.uk/government/publications/searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names/practice-guide-74-searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names>

Section 21 FOIA exemption: Information accessible to the applicant by other means

Where information held on the register of title is available for inspection through these statutory routes of access it is exempt from disclosure under section 21(2)(b) of FOIA.

Section 21 states:

“21 Information accessible to applicant by other means.

(1) Information which is reasonably accessible to the applicant otherwise than under section 1 is exempt information.

(2) For the purposes of subsection (1)—

(a) information may be reasonably accessible to the applicant even though it is accessible only on payment, and

(b) information is to be taken to be reasonably accessible to the applicant if it is information which the public authority or any other person is obliged by or under any enactment to communicate (otherwise than by making the information available for inspection) to members of the public on request, whether free of charge or on payment.”

Therefore, we are unable to provide information held on our register through FOIA, as it covered by this exemption.

Advice and assistance

Under Section 16 of FOIA and in accordance with the Section 45 FOIA code of practice, we have a duty to provide you with reasonable advice and assistance.

Please note that the ICO has previously reviewed HM Land Registry’s use of the section 21 exemption. Relevant decision notices can be accessed here<https://icosearch.ico.org.uk/s/search.html?collection=ico-meta&profile=decisions&query&query=&f.By+authority%7CpublicAuthority=HM%20Land%20Registry&f.By+section%7CsectionOfLegislation=FOI%2021> including IC-173302-N4J1<https://ico.org.uk/media/action-weve-taken/decision-notices/2022/4022883/ic-173302-n4j1.pdf>, FS50685812<https://ico.org.uk/media/action-weve-taken/decision-notices/2017/2172810/fs50685812.pdf> and FER0454056<https://ico.org.uk/media/action-weve-taken/decision-notices/2012/780474/fer_0454056.pdf>.

The ICO has agreed that this position is long established, and the Commissioner is satisfied that section 21 would be engaged for this type of request.

For assistance on how to obtain official copies of documents you can contact our Customer Support Centre by telephone between 8am and 5pm, Monday to Thursday on [phone redacted] or online through our Contact Us<https://customerhelp.landregistry.gov.uk/guide-page-external/?stepid=2b31bc48-eb96-eb11-b1ac-002248413956> form.

Our Customer Support colleagues are trained to handle queries which relate to information that is held on the register of title.

Information about how to apply to inspect or obtain official copies is contained with practice guide 11:

www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies<http://www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies>

If you need any support completing the application form for official copies or to determine which documents to order, you may contact our Customer Support colleagues:

www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry<http://www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry>

You may also refer to our Publication Scheme which includes information about how to access information that is held on the register of title under the heading ‘Request information’:

www.gov.uk/government/organisations/land-registry/about/publication-scheme#request-information<http://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/land-registry/about/publication-scheme#request-information>

Please refer to HMLR’s Transaction Data webpage which contains information in respect of commonly used abbreviations:

www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-transaction-data#abbreviations-used-in-transaction-data<http://www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-transaction-data#abbreviations-used-in-transaction-data>

If you need any independent advice about individual’s rights under information legislation you can contact the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO). The ICO is the UK’s independent authority set up to uphold information rights in the public interest, promoting openness by public bodies and data privacy for individuals.

The contact details for the ICO are detailed below. There is useful information on the ICO website which explains the rights of individuals:

www.ico.org.uk/for-the-public<http://www.ico.org.uk/for-the-public>

Please refer to the top tips:

www.ico.org.uk/for-the-public/official-information<http://www.ico.org.uk/for-the-public/official-information/>

Register information and your data protection rights

Data protection law permits HM Land Registry to use personal data for our official purposes.

The lawful basis for HM Land Registry processing personal data under the United Kingdom (UK) General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR) is that it is necessary to enable us to perform our public task of the registration of land and property (Article 6(1)(e) of UK GDPR). This is defined in the Land Registration Act 2002.

Paragraph 5 of Schedule 2 Part 1 of the Data Protection Act 2018 provides the following exemption from the specified UK GDPR provisions:

“The listed UK GDPR provisions do not apply to personal data consisting of information that the controller is obliged by an enactment to make available to the public, to the extent that the application of those provisions would prevent the controller from complying with that obligation.”

The Land Registration Act 2002 is the principal legislation governing land registration in England and Wales. It sets out provisions for the keeping of a register of title to land and requirements for its administration by HM Land Registry under a Chief Land Registrar.

The Chief Land Registrar is required by the Land Registration Act 2002 and to make register information (including any documents held on the register of title) available to the public, therefore the following data protection provisions do not apply:


  *   the requirement to provide ‘privacy notices’ to individuals
  *   the requirement to provide personal data in response to subject access requests
  *   the requirement to rectification
  *   the requirement to comply with requests to erasure (right to be ‘forgotten’)
  *   most of the principles of UK GDPR


Please visit our website for further information about our registers:

www.gov.uk/get-information-about-property-and-land<https://www.gov.uk/get-information-about-property-and-land>

For further information in relation to your rights and how HMLR processes personal data please refer to our Personal Information Charter:

www.gov.uk/government/organisations/land-registry/about/personal-information-charter<http://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/land-registry/about/personal-information-charter>




HM Land Registry’s purpose is to protect your land ownership and provide services and data that underpin an efficient and informed property market. Our vision is: “A world-leading property market as part of a thriving economy and a sustainable future”.

We welcome correspondence in English and Welsh.
